MA-Q-0117.stem: A patient returns an unopened insulin glargine package that the pharmacy dispensed in error. The patient says it stayed refrigerated, and the pharmacy can document the temperature history. The manager wants to put it back into saleable inventory. What is the best response under the Massachusetts returned-medication rule?

choices.text: Return it to saleable inventory because an unopened package is automatically eligible for redispensing.
Return it to inventory after a pharmacist confirms that the temperature history stayed within labeled storage conditions.
The pharmacy may accept the qualifying return, but it should quarantine the product rather than return it to inventory and arrange proper disposition.
Redispense it only to a patient whose prescription is for the same insulin strength and quantity.
Refuse to accept the product because Massachusetts never permits a pharmacy to receive medication it dispensed in error.

explanation.core_reasoning: The rule distinguishes accepting a qualifying returned medication from making that medication saleable again. A product dispensed in error may be accepted, but it must be quarantined and properly disposed of rather than returned to inventory for another patient.

choice_analysis.A: An intact package does not override the no-return-to-inventory rule for this qualifying returned medication.
choice_analysis.B: Good storage evidence may inform product quality, but it does not convert this patient return into saleable inventory under the cited rule.
choice_analysis.C: Acceptance, quarantine, exclusion from inventory, and proper disposition are the operative steps for the returned product described.
choice_analysis.D: Matching another patient’s prescription does not authorize redispensing a qualifying patient return.
choice_analysis.E: The regulation permits acceptance in specified circumstances, including medication dispensed in error; the restriction concerns what happens afterward.

related_facts: Insulin glargine is temperature sensitive, but storage integrity and legal inventory eligibility are different questions.
Quarantine prevents a returned product from reentering active stock while disposition is arranged.
explanation.mpje_trap: ‘Unopened and properly refrigerated’ can address quality without answering whether the law permits the patient-returned product back into inventory.

reasoning_steps: Identify why the return qualifies for pharmacy acceptance
Separate product-condition evidence from legal inventory eligibility
Apply quarantine and proper-disposition requirements

MA-Q-0118.stem: An otherwise complete Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription for insulin glargine arrives with two blank fields: the patient’s name and the directions for use. Which conclusion best addresses the defect before dispensing?

choices.text: Both blanks may be ignored because Schedule VI prescriptions are exempt from required prescription content.
The patient name is required, but directions for use are optional whenever the drug is insulin.
Directions for use are required, but patient identification is optional if the pharmacy recognizes the patient.
Both patient identification and directions are required prescription elements, so the missing information must be resolved before lawful dispensing.
The blanks matter only if the patient’s insurer refuses to adjudicate the claim.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts Schedule VI is still part of the state controlled-substance prescription framework. Patient identification and directions for use are required prescription information; familiarity with the patient or the drug does not make those elements optional.

choice_analysis.A: Schedule VI status does not create a blanket exemption from Massachusetts prescription-content requirements.
choice_analysis.B: Insulin does not make directions for use an optional field under the cited prescription-elements rule.
choice_analysis.C: Knowing the patient personally does not substitute for required patient identification on the prescription.
choice_analysis.D: The two omissions concern required elements and must be addressed rather than treated as billing details.
choice_analysis.E: Prescription validity is a legal issue independent of whether a payer will process the claim.

related_facts: Insulin glargine is prescription-only and falls within Massachusetts Schedule VI rather than federal Schedules I-V.
Massachusetts Schedule VI has no federal Schedule VI counterpart.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not let a familiar drug or familiar patient turn mandatory prescription content into optional data.

reasoning_steps: Classify the product within the Massachusetts prescription framework
Identify each omitted field as a required prescription element
Require the defect to be resolved before dispensing

MA-Q-0119.stem: A pharmacy’s software marks an alprazolam prescription for deletion seven months after it was issued because the prescription can no longer be used for refills. The pharmacy has no separate serious-event record tied to this prescription. What is the best response under Massachusetts record-retention law?

choices.text: Delete it because the end of a refill-use window automatically ends every record-retention duty.
Keep the controlled-substance prescription for the required two-year retention period; refill usability and record retention are different clocks.
Delete it if the prescriber confirms that no more refills will be authorized.
Keep it for five years because every controlled-substance prescription uses the serious-event record period.
Retention is unnecessary once the pharmacy has scanned the prescription into an electronic profile.

explanation.core_reasoning: A prescription’s ability to support additional dispensing and the pharmacy’s duty to preserve the prescription record are separate legal questions. Massachusetts requires controlled-substance prescriptions to be retained for two years, so a seven-month-old alprazolam record cannot be purged merely because a refill window has ended.

choice_analysis.A: A dispensing or refill deadline does not function as the record-destruction date.
choice_analysis.B: The pharmacy must preserve the controlled-prescription record for the separate two-year period required for inspection.
choice_analysis.C: A prescriber’s future refill intentions do not shorten the statutory retention period for the existing record.
choice_analysis.D: Five years applies to a different record category, such as records relating to certain reportable serious events, not every controlled prescription.
choice_analysis.E: Electronic storage can be a record format, but it does not eliminate the underlying retention duty.

related_facts: Alprazolam is Schedule IV.
Prescription validity, refill limits, and record preservation frequently use different legal clocks.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not delete a record merely because the prescription can no longer be used.

reasoning_steps: Classify alprazolam as a controlled prescription record
Separate refill usability from record retention
Apply the two-year preservation period

MA-Q-0120.stem: A patient asks Pharmacy B to obtain a Massachusetts warfarin prescription from Pharmacy A. The prescription was issued 10 months ago and has three authorized refills remaining. Pharmacy B has a certified pharmacy technician available, and the pharmacist on duty approves the technician’s participation. Which statements are consistent with the current Massachusetts transfer framework? Select ALL that apply.

choices.text: The pharmacies should act on the patient’s transfer request in a timely manner rather than impose a blanket no-transfer rule.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions, and the remaining authorized refills may be transferred while the prescription is within the one-year limit.
A certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI prescription transfer when the pharmacist on duty approves the activity.
Massachusetts requires the transferring pharmacy to charge the patient a transfer fee before releasing the prescription.
The transfer is barred solely because the prescription is more than six months old, even though it was issued less than one year ago.

explanation.core_reasoning: Current 247 CMR 9.14 requires timely transfer at the patient’s request, permits Schedule VI transfers using the Schedule III-V transfer framework, allows transfer of remaining refills, bars Schedule VI transfers after one year from issuance, and prohibits a transfer fee. Separately, 247 CMR 8.04 permits a certified pharmacy technician to perform Schedule VI transfers with pharmacist-on-duty approval.

choice_analysis.A: The current rule affirmatively requires a timely response to the patient or agent’s transfer request.
choice_analysis.B: At 10 months, the Schedule VI prescription remains inside the one-year transfer window and can carry its remaining authorized refills through the transfer pathway.
choice_analysis.C: The certified-technician provision is specific to Schedule VI and depends on pharmacist-on-duty approval.
choice_analysis.D: The Massachusetts rule states that a pharmacy shall not charge a prescription-transfer fee.
choice_analysis.E: The six-month concept should not be imported into the current one-year Schedule VI transfer limit.

related_facts: Warfarin is a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drug because it is not federally scheduled.
Federal controlled-substance transfer rules should not be overgeneralized into a pharmacist-only rule for Massachusetts Schedule VI transfers.
explanation.mpje_trap: Identify both the prescription’s schedule and the worker’s credential before deciding who may perform the transfer and whether the prescription is still transferable.

reasoning_steps: Classify warfarin as Massachusetts Schedule VI and check the one-year age limit
Determine what happens to remaining refills and the transfer fee
Apply the certified-technician Schedule VI transfer authority with pharmacist approval

MA-Q-0121.stem: A Rhode Island practitioner who is properly authorized for the drug issued pregabalin 20 days ago. A Massachusetts pharmacist verifies the practitioner and prescription and finds no other defect. Which conclusion best applies to dispensing in Massachusetts?

choices.text: The prescription is too old because all out-of-state controlled prescriptions expire after seven days.
The prescription may use the Massachusetts out-of-state Schedule III-VI pathway because it is within 30 days and the Schedule V verification requirement has been satisfied.
The prescription must be rewritten by a Massachusetts practitioner even after successful verification.
Pregabalin is Schedule II, so only the Massachusetts out-of-state Schedule II narcotic rule can apply.
The prescription is valid for one year in Massachusetts simply because the issuing practitioner is licensed in Rhode Island.

explanation.core_reasoning: Pregabalin is Schedule V. Massachusetts allows qualifying out-of-state Schedule III through VI prescriptions to be filled within 30 days of issuance, and the pharmacist must verify Schedule III-V prescriptions. The stem supplies both the timing and verification predicates.

choice_analysis.A: A seven-day blanket expiration rule does not describe the Schedule III-VI pathway used here.
choice_analysis.B: The 20-day age and completed verification fit the Massachusetts requirements stated for an out-of-state Schedule V prescription.
choice_analysis.C: The statute does not require a Massachusetts practitioner to rewrite every qualifying out-of-state Schedule III-VI prescription.
choice_analysis.D: Pregabalin is Schedule V, so the Schedule II-specific pathway is the wrong classification.
choice_analysis.E: Out-of-state status does not create a one-year Massachusetts dispensing window for this pathway.

related_facts: Pregabalin is federally Schedule V.
Schedule classification determines which Massachusetts out-of-state prescription rule applies.
explanation.mpje_trap: First classify the drug, then apply the out-of-state time and verification rules that belong to that schedule.

reasoning_steps: Classify pregabalin as Schedule V
Apply the 30-day out-of-state Schedule III-VI limit
Confirm that the Schedule III-V verification step is satisfied

MA-Q-0122.stem: A pharmacy system sees ‘Massachusetts Schedule VI’ on a gabapentin record and automatically applies federal Schedule II ordering rules and federal Schedule III-V refill limits. Which correction is most accurate?

choices.text: Keep the federal flags because every Massachusetts Schedule VI drug is also a federal Schedule II drug.
Remove all prescription controls because Schedule VI means over-the-counter under federal law.

Treat Schedule VI as a Massachusetts prescription-drug category with no federal Schedule VI counterpart; do not import federal Schedule II or III-V consequences solely from the state Schedule VI label.
Convert gabapentin to federal Schedule IV whenever it is dispensed in Massachusetts.
Apply federal Form 222 ordering to every Massachusetts prescription drug that is not listed in federal Schedules III-V.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts Schedule VI captures prescription drugs not included in Schedules I-V and has no federal Schedule VI counterpart. State Schedule VI status can create Massachusetts prescription-law obligations, but it does not by itself make gabapentin federal Schedule II or subject it to federal Schedule III-V rules.

choice_analysis.A: The state Schedule VI label does not convert a drug into federal Schedule II.
choice_analysis.B: Schedule VI is a prescription-drug category, not an OTC category.
choice_analysis.C: This preserves Massachusetts regulation while preventing a state classification from being mistaken for a federal controlled-substance schedule.
choice_analysis.D: Dispensing location does not reclassify gabapentin into federal Schedule IV.
choice_analysis.E: Form 222/CSOS requirements turn on federal Schedule I-II distribution, not Massachusetts Schedule VI status.

related_facts: Gabapentin is not federally scheduled and is treated as a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription drug.
State and federal scheduling systems can create different consequences for the same product.
explanation.mpje_trap: The Roman numeral ‘VI’ is a Massachusetts category, not a missing sixth federal controlled-substance schedule.

reasoning_steps: Identify Massachusetts Schedule VI as a state classification
Check gabapentin’s separate federal scheduling status
Reject federal Schedule II or III-V consequences that arise only from the incorrect state-to-federal translation

MA-Q-0123.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives an otherwise valid written methylphenidate prescription. The prescriber indicates that a state electronic-prescribing exception or waiver applies, but the pharmacist has no practical way to verify whether the prescriber properly qualifies for that exception. What does 105 CMR 721.070(C) require of the pharmacist on that specific issue?

choices.text: The pharmacist is not required to verify that an otherwise valid written or oral prescription properly falls within an electronic-prescribing exception or waiver.
The pharmacist must independently prove the prescriber’s exception before considering any other prescription-validity requirement.
The pharmacist must reject every nonelectronic controlled-substance prescription even when an exception or waiver may apply.
The pharmacist must contact the Board for case-by-case permission before dispensing any written prescription.
The pharmacist may ignore all other controlled-substance requirements once the prescriber mentions an electronic-prescribing exception.

explanation.core_reasoning: Massachusetts places the electronic-prescribing compliance obligation on the prescriber without making the dispensing pharmacist the verifier of the prescriber’s exception or waiver. Section 721.070(C) says the pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that exception status. Other prescription requirements still apply.

choice_analysis.A: This states the pharmacist-facing no-verification rule in 105 CMR 721.070(C).
choice_analysis.B: The regulation expressly avoids imposing that exception-verification duty on the pharmacist receiving an otherwise valid prescription.
choice_analysis.C: Exceptions and waivers are part of the framework, so nonelectronic form alone is not an automatic pharmacist-side rejection rule.
choice_analysis.D: The regulation does not require routine Board preclearance for each otherwise valid written prescription.
choice_analysis.E: No-verification of the e-prescribing exception does not waive schedule, legitimacy, content, or other dispensing requirements.

related_facts: Methylphenidate is federal Schedule II.
The prescriber’s e-prescribing obligation and the pharmacist’s duty to assess the prescription’s other legal requirements are distinct questions.
explanation.mpje_trap: ‘Not required to verify the exception’ is not the same as ‘not required to verify anything about the prescription.’

reasoning_steps: Identify that the question is limited to the prescriber’s e-prescribing exception or waiver
Apply the pharmacist-facing no-verification rule
Preserve all other prescription and controlled-substance requirements

MA-Q-0124.stem: A properly authorized New Hampshire practitioner telephones a lawful alprazolam prescription to a Massachusetts pharmacist. The pharmacist verifies the Schedule IV prescription under the out-of-state pathway. A staff member says the pharmacy must wait for a written prescription before dispensing. Which response is most accurate?

choices.text: Treat the call as a Schedule II emergency prescription and require the Schedule II follow-up process before any dispensing.

The lawful oral Schedule III-V pathway may be used; the pharmacist should record a request to the practitioner for a written prescription within seven days or any shorter federal period that controls.
Dispense now and wait six months before asking the practitioner for any written record.
Ask the patient to create and sign the written follow-up because the original prescription was oral.
Reject every out-of-state oral Schedule III-V prescription because Massachusetts recognizes only electronic out-of-state prescriptions.

explanation.core_reasoning: Alprazolam is Schedule IV, so the Massachusetts out-of-state oral Schedule III-V pathway applies rather than the Schedule II emergency framework. The pharmacist records the required request to the practitioner for the written prescription within seven days or any shorter federal period that applies.

choice_analysis.A: Schedule II emergency follow-up rules should not be transplanted onto a Schedule IV prescription.
choice_analysis.B: This uses the correct schedule-specific oral pathway and identifies the Massachusetts follow-up record action.
choice_analysis.C: A six-month refill concept is unrelated to the short written-follow-up request in this setting.
choice_analysis.D: The authorized practitioner, not the patient, is the source of the follow-up prescription record.
choice_analysis.E: Massachusetts law expressly contemplates qualifying oral out-of-state Schedule III-V prescriptions.

related_facts: Alprazolam is Schedule IV.
Oral prescription rules vary by schedule; seeing the word ‘oral’ is not enough to choose the Schedule II emergency rule.
explanation.mpje_trap: Classify the drug before choosing the oral-prescription follow-up pathway.

reasoning_steps: Classify alprazolam as Schedule IV
Apply the out-of-state Schedule III-V oral prescription pathway
Identify the written-follow-up request and timing rule

MA-Q-0125.stem: A new pharmacy’s DEA registration becomes effective July 1, but the pharmacy does not receive or otherwise begin handling any controlled substances until July 10. Which date controls the federal initial controlled-substance inventory under 21 CFR 1304.11(b)?

choices.text: July 1, solely because the registration became effective on that date.
July 5, because every new registration receives a four-day grace period.
July 10, when the registrant first engages in controlled-substance activity.
The last day of July, because initial inventories are always month-end records.
Two years after July 1, because the biennial inventory replaces the initial inventory.

explanation.core_reasoning: The federal initial-inventory trigger is the date the registrant first engages in controlled-substance activity, not merely the effective date printed on the registration. Here, that first activity occurs July 10.

choice_analysis.A: Registration status is necessary, but the cited initial-inventory timing rule is keyed to first controlled-substance activity.
choice_analysis.B: The regulation does not create the proposed four-day grace period.
choice_analysis.C: July 10 is the first day the facts show the registrant engaging in controlled-substance activity.
choice_analysis.D: The rule is event-based rather than tied to month-end accounting.
choice_analysis.E: The biennial cycle follows the initial inventory and cannot replace it.

related_facts: Initial and biennial inventories are separate federal duties.
A registration date and the first controlled-substance activity date can be different.
explanation.mpje_trap: When two dates are given, identify which event the regulation actually uses as its trigger.

reasoning_steps: Separate registration effective date from first controlled-substance activity
Apply the federal event-based initial-inventory trigger

MA-Q-0126.stem: A pharmacy completed a controlled-substance inventory on January 15, 2025. Management proposes making the next required inventory on July 15, 2027 because the store also performs monthly cycle counts. Which statement best evaluates that plan under the federal biennial inventory rule?

choices.text: The plan is acceptable because monthly cycle counts permit a 30-month gap between required inventories.
The plan is acceptable whenever the pharmacy has no Schedule II stock on the later date.
The plan is acceptable because ‘biennial’ means twice during any five-year period.
The required inventory cannot be deferred beyond the at-least-every-two-years interval; internal cycle counts do not create a longer federal interval.
The next required inventory must occur exactly six months after January 15, 2025.

explanation.core_reasoning: After the initial inventory, federal law requires a new controlled-substance inventory at least every two years. A pharmacy can count more often for operational reasons, but monthly cycle counts do not authorize extending the required inventory interval to 30 months.

choice_analysis.A: Additional internal counts can be more frequent than federal requirements but do not lengthen the maximum interval between required inventories.
choice_analysis.B: The biennial inventory obligation is not switched off simply because one schedule happens to be absent.
choice_analysis.C: Biennial means every two years in this regulation, not two inventories somewhere within five years.
choice_analysis.D: A July 2027 required inventory would exceed two years from January 15, 2025, so the proposed schedule is too late.
choice_analysis.E: Federal law permits a longer interval than six months; the maximum is two years.

related_facts: A pharmacy may conduct controlled-substance inventories more frequently than the federal minimum schedule.
Operational cycle counts and the legally required inventory are not automatically the same record.
explanation.mpje_trap: More frequent internal counting does not buy extra time before the legally required inventory.

reasoning_steps: Identify the date of the last required inventory
Compare the proposed next date with the two-year maximum interval
Distinguish internal cycle counts from the required federal inventory

MA-Q-0127.stem: During a federal inventory, the pharmacy finds three opened stock containers: Adderall (Schedule II), a 500-tablet alprazolam container, and a 2,000-tablet alprazolam container. Which counting approaches are permitted or required? Select ALL that apply.

choices.text: Estimate the opened Adderall quantity because the original bottle contained fewer than 1,000 tablets.
Count or measure the Schedule II Adderall quantity exactly.
The opened 500-tablet Schedule IV alprazolam container may generally be estimated.
The opened 2,000-tablet Schedule IV alprazolam container may be estimated solely because alprazolam is not Schedule II.
Use an exact count for the opened Schedule IV alprazolam container holding more than 1,000 tablets.

explanation.core_reasoning: Federal inventory counting uses both schedule and container size. Schedule II quantities require an exact count or measure. Opened Schedule III-V containers may generally be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, in which case an exact count is required.

choice_analysis.A: The opened-container estimation allowance does not replace the exact-count requirement for Schedule II inventory.
choice_analysis.B: Adderall is Schedule II, so its inventory quantity must be counted or measured exactly.
choice_analysis.C: An opened Schedule IV container at or below the 1,000-unit threshold may generally be estimated.
choice_analysis.D: Schedule IV status alone is not enough; the over-1,000-unit container crosses the threshold for exact counting.
choice_analysis.E: The 2,000-tablet Schedule IV container exceeds the threshold and therefore requires an exact count.

related_facts: Adderall contains amphetamine salts and is Schedule II.
Alprazolam is Schedule IV, so container size determines whether estimation is permitted for an opened container.
explanation.mpje_trap: Use two variables, not one: first schedule, then container size for opened Schedule III-V stock.

reasoning_steps: Classify Adderall and alprazolam by schedule
Apply the exact-count rule to Schedule II
Apply the 1,000-unit threshold separately to each opened Schedule IV container

MA-Q-0128.stem: A pharmacy places one wholesaler order containing alprazolam and methylphenidate. The wholesaler’s ordinary commercial ordering system can handle the alprazolam line but asks what additional federal ordering mechanism is needed for the other drug. Which response is correct?

choices.text: Use DEA Form 41 for methylphenidate because Form 41 is the routine Schedule II purchasing form.
Use DEA Form 106 for methylphenidate because every Schedule II acquisition is treated as a theft-or-loss event.
Use DEA Form 222 or a compliant digitally signed CSOS order for the methylphenidate Schedule II distribution, absent an applicable exception.
Use Form 222 for alprazolam only because Schedule IV drugs have stricter ordering rules than Schedule II drugs.
No controlled-substance ordering record is needed for either line because both drugs have accepted medical uses.

explanation.core_reasoning: The mixed order must be classified drug by drug. Methylphenidate is Schedule II and generally requires DEA Form 222 or a compliant CSOS electronic order for distribution. Alprazolam is Schedule IV and does not trigger the Schedule I-II Form 222/CSOS ordering requirement merely by appearing on the same purchase.

choice_analysis.A: Form 41 is associated with controlled-substance destruction rather than routine Schedule II procurement.
choice_analysis.B: Form 106 addresses theft or significant loss, not ordinary purchasing.
choice_analysis.C: This matches the federal ordering mechanism triggered by the methylphenidate Schedule II line.
choice_analysis.D: The Form 222/CSOS rule applies to Schedule I-II distribution, not Schedule IV alprazolam solely because it is controlled.
choice_analysis.E: Accepted medical use does not remove the procurement controls attached to Schedule II distribution.

related_facts: Methylphenidate is Schedule II.
Alprazolam is Schedule IV, so the two drugs in the same commercial order can require different controlled-substance records.
explanation.mpje_trap: A wholesaler order can contain multiple schedules; apply the procurement rule to each line rather than to the invoice as a whole.

reasoning_steps: Classify methylphenidate and alprazolam separately
Identify which line is a Schedule II distribution
Choose the Form 222 or CSOS pathway for that line

MA-Q-0129.stem: During an audit, a pharmacy finds that its paper DEA Form 222 records are mixed into ordinary purchase invoices, while its electronic Form 222 records are stored in a system that can retrieve them immediately and separately from other records. Which assessment is most accurate?

choices.text: Both systems are compliant because paper and electronic Form 222 records use exactly the same filing mechanics.

The paper filing needs correction because paper Form 222 records must be maintained separately for the required period, while readily retrievable electronic records can satisfy the separate-maintenance concept electronically.
Only the electronic system is defective because federal law requires every Form 222 to be stored as an original paper document.
The pharmacy may discard all Form 222 records after receiving the wholesaler shipment if it keeps ordinary invoices.
The distinction matters only for Schedule IV purchases because Schedule II orders do not have a Form 222 record-retention rule.

explanation.core_reasoning: Federal Form 222 preservation rules distinguish paper from electronic records. Paper forms must be separately maintained for the required two-year period. Electronic Form 222 records are treated as separately maintained when they are readily retrievable from other records, so the two systems should not be forced into identical physical filing mechanics.

choice_analysis.A: The federal rule deliberately distinguishes paper separate maintenance from electronic readily retrievable treatment.
choice_analysis.B: The paper records are improperly mixed, while the described electronic system satisfies the distinct readily retrievable concept.
choice_analysis.C: A compliant electronic Form 222 record need not be converted into an original paper form merely to satisfy record preservation.
choice_analysis.D: Purchase invoices do not substitute for the specific Form 222 preservation duty.
choice_analysis.E: Form 222 concerns Schedule I-II ordering; Schedule IV is not the schedule that creates this Form 222 record rule.

related_facts: The recordkeeping question follows the procurement transaction after the order is completed.
‘Separately maintained’ is implemented differently for paper and electronic Form 222 records.
explanation.mpje_trap: Do not copy the paper filing rule word-for-word onto a compliant electronic record system.

reasoning_steps: Identify the record format for each set of Form 222 records
Apply separate maintenance to paper records
Apply the readily retrievable standard to the electronic records
